name: Point & Grasp
summary: To select an out-of-reach object, the user points at it and shapes the hand as if to grasp it; a Bayesian model combines the pointing direction with a learned grasp-gesture likelihood and selects the most probable object.
howItWorks: Each cue gives a likelihood over the scene's objects: the pointing direction by the angle between the hand ray and each object, and the grasp posture by a neural model trained on the Out-of-Reach Grasping (ORG) dataset collected from 19 people, matching hand configuration to object shape. Bayes' rule fuses them into a posterior and the object with the maximum posterior is selected, so a cluttered layout can be resolved by shape and similar-shaped objects by direction. In the Quest 2 hand-tracking studies the right hand pointed and grasped and the left pressed the space bar to confirm. Study 1 (12 participants) showed it faster and more accurate than pointing or grasping alone; Study 2 (12 participants), with a ray-end cursor added, was faster than Expand under low spatial ambiguity and faster than BubbleRay under high spatial ambiguity, with completion rates close to Expand and well above BubbleRay.
advantages: Robust when one cue is ambiguous: shape separates crowded objects, direction separates similar-shaped ones.
No refinement step, so it avoids Expand's overhead in sparse layouts.
Runs in real time; grasping felt natural and easy to learn.
limitations: Needs a trained gesture model and object shape information.
Confirmation used a keyboard key in the studies.
Less accurate than Expand when objects are both crowded and similar in shape.

relationships.note: Study 2: faster under high spatial ambiguity and a higher completion rate.
Study 2: faster under low spatial ambiguity; Expand was slightly more accurate.
Pointing direction is one of the two fused cues.
Also uses the grasp posture to infer the target.

review.notes: Coded from the CHI 2026 full text. Framed as mixed reality, but the studies ran in VR on a Quest 2. Confirmation was a keyboard space bar pressed by the other hand; the authors note it could be replaced. Occlusion coded partly: occluded layouts were part of the high spatial ambiguity condition.
